meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Gehrig. But it opened the speech, it did not close it — the 1942 film moved it — and the newspapers disagreed about the words.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1903–1941 · New York Yankees first baseman · Baseball Hall of Fame, 1939
answer.sourceLine: Gehrig said it at Yankee Stadium on 4 July 1939, between games of a doubleheader against the Washington Senators, at the ceremony the Yankees called Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day. The Evening Star of Washington printed this exact sentence the following morning, in an Associated Press despatch by Sid Feder. Note where it sits: near the start of the address, not the end — the ending everyone remembers belongs to Gary Cooper and the 1942 film.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 4 July 1939 — Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day, Yankee Stadium, before 61,808 fans
A newsreel snippet of four sentences. There is no recording of the whole address.

source.excerpt: Several times his voice broke and a sob escaped as he announced, “Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth.”
trail: The exact sentence is in print within twenty-four hours. The Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), 5 July 1939, page 14 ↗ carries Sid Feder’s Associated Press report of the ceremony and quotes Gehrig directly: “Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth.”

A second wire service covered the same speech and took it down differently. The Washington Daily News of the same date ↗ and the Waterbury Democrat ↗ both ran Leslie Avery’s United Press despatch, which has Gehrig saying “For the past two weeks you’ve been reading about what a bad break I had. But I want to say now that I’m the luckiest man on the face of the earth.”

There is no tape to settle it. Steve Wulf, writing for ESPN on the speech’s 75th anniversary ↗, records that “only a small snippet of the newsreel footage, only four sentences, has survived” — so every full text of the address is assembled from press accounts.

The line opened the speech. Wulf again: it “came at the very beginning of Gehrig’s speech, but for dramatic effect, it’s at the end of Cooper’s” in The Pride of the Yankees (1942). The Evening Star’s report bears that out — the quotation comes first, and Gehrig’s remarks about his old team-mates follow it.

Wikiquote’s sourced Gehrig page ↗ and Wikipedia ↗ both attribute the line to the 4 July 1939 speech; Wikipedia footnotes the competing readings (“Yet today”, “this” for “the”) rather than choosing between them.
source.excerptNote: That is the Associated Press wording, read from the Library of Congress’s scan of the Evening Star of 5 July 1939 ↗. The United Press filed the same sentence differently the same day — “I want to say now that I’m the luckiest man on the face of the earth” ↗ — and the full texts that circulate today mostly read “the face of this earth.” All three agree on the phrase people actually remember.

author.name: Lou Gehrig
author.heading: About Lou Gehrig
author.metaLine: 1903–1941 · New York Yankees first baseman · Baseball Hall of Fame, 1939
author.bio: Henry Louis “Lou” Gehrig (19 June 1903 – 2 June 1941) played seventeen seasons at first base for the New York Yankees and was nicknamed “the Iron Horse” for a streak of 2,130 consecutive games that stood for fifty-six years. He took himself out of the lineup on 2 May 1939; the Mayo Clinic’s diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis was made public on his thirty-sixth birthday, 19 June, and the Yankees held Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day two weeks later. He died less than two years afterwards, and in the United States the disease still carries his name.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Gehrig said this. What almost everybody has wrong is where in the speech it came, and which words surrounded it.

items.why: Gary Cooper’s screen version ends on the line, and that is the version most people carry in their heads. Wulf ↗ is explicit: it “came at the very beginning of Gehrig’s speech, but for dramatic effect, it’s at the end of Cooper’s.” The film’s speech is 169 words to Gehrig’s 277.
The full texts in wide circulation — the estate’s own site ↗ and Sports Illustrated ↗ — read “this earth”. Both 1939 wire reports read “the earth”, and Wikiquote ↗ follows them.

The UP transcription has no “I consider myself” at all: “I want to say now that I’m the luckiest man on the face of the earth.” Two reporters, one microphone, two sentences — which is what happens when only four sentences of film survive ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Gehrig said it, on 4 July 1939, and the Associated Press printed this exact sentence the next morning — see the Evening Star for 5 July 1939 ↗. He said it at the start of the speech, not the end.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Gehrig had taken himself out of the Yankees’ lineup on 2 May 1939 after 2,130 straight games, and the Mayo Clinic’s diagnosis became public on his thirty-sixth birthday. Two weeks later the club filled Yankee Stadium to say goodbye to him. He had not meant to speak at all; the master of ceremonies had already told the crowd he was too moved to.

Then he did, and the sentence he opened with inverted the whole occasion: sixty-one thousand people had come to pity him, and he told them he was lucky. The papers the next morning could not agree on the words, but every one of them led with that.
detailsBody: The Associated Press man, Sid Feder, filed a piece that is mostly about Babe Ruth — the two had not spoken in years — putting an arm round Gehrig and whispering “C’mon, kid, buck up now. We’re all with you.” Feder ends with Gehrig stumbling back to the clubhouse asking, “Did my speech sound silly? Did it?”

The reason the wordings differ is that there is almost nothing to check them against. Four sentences of newsreel survive. Samuel Goldwyn, who did not much like baseball, agreed to make The Pride of the Yankees after being shown that footage; his director then rewrote the speech over the objections of both the film’s editor and Eleanor Gehrig, who wrote to him: “I feel if you should depart from the original you would lose all of the simple charm.”
context.pull: Sixty-one thousand people came to pity him. He opened by telling them he was the lucky one.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), 5 July 1939, page 14, in an Associated Press report by Sid Feder, prints: 'Several times his voice broke and a sob escaped as he announced, "Today I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth."'

The Washington Daily News, 5 July 1939, page 28, prints a different transcription: 'For the past two weeks,' he said, 'you've been reading about what a bad break I had. But I want to say now that I'm the luckiest man on the face of the earth.'

The Waterbury Democrat (Waterbury, Conn.), 5 July 1939, page 16, in a United Press report by Leslie Avery headlined 'LOU GEHRIG CRIES AS 62,000 FANS STAND TO CHEER', prints the same United Press wording as the Washington Daily News.

Steve Wulf, ESPN, 4 July 2014: 'only a small snippet of the newsreel footage, only four sentences, has survived'; the 'luckiest man' line 'came at the very beginning of Gehrig's speech, but for dramatic effect, it's at the end of Cooper's' in the 1942 film The Pride of the Yankees; the real address runs 277 words to the film's 169.

Wikiquote's Lou Gehrig page sources both 'Fans, for the past two weeks you have been reading about a bad break I got. Yet today, I consider myself the luckiest man on the face of the earth' and 'So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I've got an awful lot to live for' to the speech made on Lou Gehrig Appreciation Day at Yankee Stadium, July 4, 1939.

The official lougehrig.com 'Farewell Address' page gives the closing sentence as 'So I close in saying that I might have been given a bad break, but I've got an awful lot to live for.' and the opening as '...the luckiest man on the face of this earth.'

Sports Illustrated's 'Full Text of Lou Gehrig's Farewell Speech', which cites lougehrig.com as its source, gives the closing sentence differently: 'So I close in saying that I may have had a tough break, but I have an awful lot to live for.'

Wikipedia's Lou Gehrig article gives the speech text with explicit footnotes recording variant readings: 'Also reported as: "...you have been reading about the bad break I got"', 'Also reported as: "Yet today"', and 'Also reported as: "this"' for 'the face of the Earth'. It gives his dates as June 19, 1903 - June 2, 1941.
